docs.title: Welcome to Bonfire
docs.text: Bonfire provides CodeIgniter 4 applications with powerful tools, and a ready-to-integrate admin area, to help you build robust applications faster. It does not aim to be a full CMS, but rather a framework to help you build your own web application or internal tools.

docs.title: Important features
docs.text:
• Powerful and flexible user authentication system, with either password or personal access tokens
  • Simple theme system with reusable component system
  • Admin area
  • Easily expandable users
  • Possibility to easily integrate modules for your own resources in admin area
  • Meta information that can be stored on your resources without changing the database tables
  • Easy to add filters to resource lists in the admin
  • Global search feature that you can easily tie your own resources into
  • Global "recycle bin" where admins can un-delete or purge soft-deleted resources
  • Cookie Consent framework to help you comply with GDPR
  • Customizable charts and stats for the dashboard
  • Easy log and system info viewers
  • A way to provide documentation with your app

docs.text: Any application admin panel will need more than just user management capabilities. Your app might need page, tag, product management. This section deals with extending Bonfire admin are with your own modules and integrating them into the admin panel.

docs.title: Creating an Admin Module
docs.text:
Learn how to create new modules of code for the admin area, centered around a single task or resource, like Users, Photos, etc. This guide covers the basics of creating a Module.php file, configuring module locations, and adding menu items.

Read more about Creating an Admin Module

docs.title: View Components
docs.text:
View Components allow you to create custom HTML elements to use within your views. This section lists the components available within the default Admin theme and provides examples of their usage.

Read more about View Components

docs.title: Filters
docs.text:
Filtering allows you to specify which columns can be filtered and then pass your model to a view cell that handles the display of the filters. This ensures a consistent look and functionality in the UI while providing the least amount of work when creating a UI.

Read more about Filters

docs.title: Recycler
docs.text:
The Recycler provides an area where users can browse objects that have been deleted and either restore or purge them. The models for these resources must have soft deletes enabled. This section covers registering a resource, localizing column names, and changing how a model is listed, restored and purged.

Read more about the Recycler

docs.title: Resource Tabs
docs.text:
Resource tabs are the tabs displayed when editing a resource, like an individual User or User Group. They make it possible to easily integrate other tabs onto a user without editing the core theme.

docs.title: Row and Bulk Actions
docs.text:
An action is something an admin can do to one record from its row's menu, or to every checked record of a list from the selection bar: delete, ban, publish, export. Bonfire runs every action through one endpoint that checks the permission and the CSRF token, asks for confirmation when the action wants it, skips records the action may not touch, and runs large batches in the background when a queue is available.

The Users list (row and bulk delete) and the Logs list (bulk delete) are built this way.

docs.title: Writing An Action
docs.text:
An action is one class that extends Bonfire\Actions\Action:

use Bonfire\Actions\Action;
use Bonfire\Actions\ActionContext;
use Bonfire\Actions\ActionResult;
use Bonfire\Actions\Confirm;
use Bonfire\Actions\Placement;
use Bonfire\Users\User;

class BanUsers extends Action
{
    public string    $label      = 'Ban';
    public string    $icon       = 'fas fa-ban';
    public string    $permission = 'users.manage-admins';
    public Placement $placement  = Placement::Both;
    public bool      $danger     = true;

    public function confirm(): ?Confirm
    {
        return Confirm::make('Ban {count} users?')
            ->body('They are signed out and cannot sign in until unbanned.')
            ->button('Ban');
    }

    public function allows(User $actor, object $record): bool
    {
        return $actor->id !== $record->id;
    }

    public function handle(ActionContext $context): ActionResult
    {
        foreach ($context->entities() as $user) {
            $user->ban();
        }

        return ActionResult::message('{count} users banned.');
    }
}

label and icon (a Font Awesome class) are shown on the action's button.

permission is needed to see and run the action. Leave it empty for anyone who can reach the admin area. Add a new permission to your app's AuthGroups config.

placement is where the action is offered: Placement::Row in each row's menu, Placement::Bulk in the selection bar, or Placement::Both.

danger styles the action as destructive, in red.

confirm() returns what to ask before the action runs, or null to run straight away. {count} in the title becomes the number of records. ->typeToConfirm() makes the admin type that number before a large destructive run.

allows() decides, per record, whether the action may touch it. Records it rejects, and selected records that no longer exist, are skipped and reported ("3 users banned. Skipped 1.") rather than failing the batch.

handle() does the work and returns an ActionResult::message(), or ActionResult::error() when it fails. {count} in the message becomes the number of records handled. A thrown exception is logged, and the admin sees an "Unknown error" message.

The action's name in its URL comes from the class name: BanUsers is ban-users.

Warning

handle() may run in a queue worker, where there is no request, session or signed-in user. Use only what the context gives you: $context->entities() (the records, one at a time), $context->chunks() (the records, a chunk of up to 100 at a time) and $context->actor() (the admin who started the run).

docs.title: Deleting
docs.text:
Bonfire\Actions\DeleteAction is a ready-made delete: a red Delete that asks first and deletes a chunk at a time. Extend it with how your records are deleted, and usually your own permission and wording:

use Bonfire\Actions\DeleteAction;

class DeletePhotos extends DeleteAction
{
    public string $permission = 'photos.delete';

    protected function delete(array $records): void
    {
        model(PhotoModel::class)->delete(array_map(static fn ($photo) => $photo->id, $records));
    }
}

Override confirm() for your own question and deleted() for the message once it's done. See Bonfire\Users\Actions\DeleteUsers for a complete example.

docs.title: Registering Actions
docs.text:
Actions belong to a named list. Register them in your module's initAdmin(), saying where the list's records come from:

use Bonfire\Actions\ModelSource;

public function initAdmin()
{
    service('actions')->for('photos')
        ->records(new ModelSource(PhotoModel::class))
        ->add(new DeletePhotos());
}

ModelSource finds records by primary key through a model. For records that don't live in a model, implement Bonfire\Actions\RecordSource, which has one method, find(array $ids): array; the Logs list's LogStore is an example.

Any module may add actions to any list, including Bonfire's own. These lists exist:

List Records users Bonfire\Users\User logs Objects whose id is a log file's name 
service('actions')->for('users')->add(new BanUsers());

docs.title: Showing Actions In A List
docs.text:
Two view components render a list's actions for the signed-in admin, leaving out those they lack the permission for.

<x-row-actions> renders a row's menu. Pass the list and the record's ID. Anything in its slot, like an Edit link, comes first:

<td class="text-end">
    <x-row-actions list="photos" id="<?= $photo->id ?>">
        <li><a href="<?= url_to('photo-edit', $photo->id) ?>" class="dropdown-item">Edit</a></li>
    </x-row-actions>
</td>

The row menu shows only the actions the admin may run on that record: their permission, and their allows() for it. To ask allows(), the component needs the record. Hand the page's records to the list with showing() before the rows render, or the component loads each one through the list's record source, one lookup per row.

<x-bulk-actions> goes inside <x-selection-bar>, in a form whose row checkboxes are named selects[] with the record's ID as their value. Ask the list's selectable() whether to show them at all: it is true when the admin may run any of its bulk actions. Given a record, it says whether any of those actions allows() it:

<?php
$actionList = service('actions')->for('photos')->showing($photos);
$selectable = $actionList->selectable(auth()->user());
?>
<form method="post">
    <?= csrf_field() ?>
    <table class="table bf-table">
        <!-- ... -->
        <?php if ($selectable) : ?>
            <td class="bf-select-cell">
                <input type="checkbox" name="selects[]" value="<?= $photo->id ?>" class="form-check-input"
                    <?= $actionList->selectable(auth()->user(), $photo) ? '' : 'disabled' ?>>
            </td>
        <?php endif ?>
        <!-- ... -->
    </table>

    <?php if ($selectable) : ?>
        <x-selection-bar>
            <x-bulk-actions list="photos" />
        </x-selection-bar>
    <?php endif ?>
</form>

docs.title: Confirmation
docs.text:
With JavaScript, an action that asks first opens <x-confirm-dialog>, a dialog that is in the Admin layout once. It shows the title with the count filled in, the body, and a red button for dangerous actions.

Without JavaScript, the action's button posts straight to the endpoint, which answers with a confirmation page holding the same question and a button to go ahead. Either way, an action never runs until it's confirmed.

The dialog also handles two other kinds of confirmation, so they look the same:

  • htmx's hx-confirm attribute: <a hx-get="..." hx-confirm="Remove the image?">.
  • A data-confirm attribute on any link or submit button: the link is followed, or the form submitted, once the admin confirms. data-confirm-button sets the button's label and data-confirm-danger="1" makes it red.
<a href="<?= url_to('photo-purge', $photo->id) ?>" data-confirm="Purge this photo?" data-confirm-danger="1">Purge</a>

docs.title: Running In The Background
docs.text:
Each action decides whether its runs are queued with its $queue property:

  • Queue::Auto (the default) runs in the request, unless it has more records than $queueAbove (500 by default).
  • Queue::Always always queues.
  • Queue::Never always runs in the request.
use Bonfire\Actions\Queue;

class ExportPhotos extends Action
{
    public Queue $queue = Queue::Always;
    // ...
}

Queued runs need the codeigniter4/queue package, which Bonfire suggests but doesn't require:

composer require codeigniter4/queue
php spark migrate --all
php spark queue:work bonfire-actions

Bonfire registers its bonfire-action job with the queue for you. Keep a queue:work bonfire-actions worker running, or queued runs will wait forever.

Without the package, Queue::Auto runs in the request, a chunk at a time, and Queue::Always refuses with a message explaining what's missing.

A queued run is recorded in the action_runs table with its totals and status. The admin who started it sees a toast that shows its progress, updated every two seconds, and its message once it ends. service('actionRuns') owns this lifecycle: the endpoint, the queue job and <x-action-run> all go through it.

docs.title: Creating an Admin Module
docs.text:
The bulk of your work in the admin area will likely be done creating new modules of code. Modules are groups of code centered around a single task or resource, like Users, Photos, etc. For the most part, admin modules are like any other bit of module CodeIgniter code, except for a new Module.php file that helps the module integrate into the admin area. Other than that you will be able to take advantage of solutions that allow your code to integrate directly into settings pages, be part of the global search results, automatically display and manage filtering of a resource list, or show up in the Recycler.

A good module to look at when creating your own is the Bonfire's own Users module (src/Users). You can also look at an example module Pages, which is an implementation of a module of Bonfire 2 admin panel for administration of pages on a website.

docs.title: Configuring Module Locations
docs.text:
In order for Bonfire to discover your modules, you need to specify one or more locations that you plan on storing the modules. By default, the system will look within app/Modules for directories. As an example, we could create a Blog folder to store our new blog package. You would then need to create the standard directories, Config, Controllers, Models and Views at the very least. A Module.php file is also expected to live here, which we will look at in more detail a little later. The directory structure would look like:

app/
    Modules/
        Blog/
            Config/
            Controllers/
            Models/
            Views/
            Module.php

All files within the Blog directory would be expected to live within the App\Modules\{ModuleName} namespace, i.e. App\Modules\Blog\Config\Routes. You can customize this by editing Config\Bonfire and changing the key of the $appModules setting within it.

public $appModules = [
    'App\Modules' => APPPATH .'Modules',
];

For example, if I would prefer the modules to simply live within my company's namespace, Acme, I could edit the key to reflect that:

public $appModules = [
    'Acme' => APPPATH .'Modules',
];

If you have multiple locations you need to keep modules, you can add multiple entries here and they will all be automatically discovered and registered within Bonfire.

docs.title: The Module File
docs.text:
The Module file handles initialization functions when the admin is loaded. It allows the module to create new menus, insert itself into the existing sidebar menus, etc. The initAdmin method is where all of the setup for displaying and admin page should be done.

namespace Acme\Blog;

use Bonfire\Core\BaseModule;
use Bonfire\Menus\MenuItem;

class Module extends BaseModule
{
    public function initAdmin()
    {
        //
    }
}

docs.title: Adding a Menu Item
docs.text:
The main side navigation in the admin consists of three primary menu collections:

  • a main Content collection where you would place the main page for managing a resource (like Users)
  • the Settings collection where your module's settings pages should live.
  • the Tools collection which holds miscellaneous things that are helpful, but not needed on a daily basis.

Menu items are added to the sidebar using the menus service. Below are two examples taken from the core Users module. They share common setup which will be discussed after the example:

// Settings menu for sidebar
$sidebar = service('menus');
$item    = new MenuItem([
    'title'           => 'Users',
    'namedRoute'      => 'user-settings',
    'fontAwesomeIcon' => 'fas fa-user',
    'permission'      => 'users.settings',
]);
$sidebar->menu('sidebar')->collection('settings')->addItem($item);

// Content Menu for sidebar
$item = new MenuItem([
    'title'           => 'Users',
    'namedRoute'      => 'user-list',
    'fontAwesomeIcon' => 'fas fa-users',
    'permission'      => 'users.list',
]);
$sidebar->menu('sidebar')->collection('content')->addItem($item);

MenuItems contain the information about a single menu item. When you create a new one you have the following settings available to you:

  • title is the string that will be displayed to the user in the Menu
  • namedRoute is the route that will be called when the link is clicked. You must use a named route which should be defined within your module's Config/Routes file.
  • fontAwesomeIcon is used to specify the FontAwesome icon that will be displayed in the sidebar.
  • permission is used to specify a permission string that is required for a user to see that link. If they do not have the proper permissions the link will not be displayed within the menu. If this item should be available to everyone leave it blank.

One the MenuItem has been created, you add it to the appropriate menu/collection.

Every menu item the user may see also shows up in the ⌘K / Ctrl+K command palette, and the header's breadcrumb names the active item (and its collection, when that collection is collapsible).

docs.title: Naming a page in the breadcrumb
docs.text:
A page below a menu item, like a single record's edit form, can add itself to the breadcrumb with a crumb view section. The breadcrumb then reads "active menu item › crumb". When the page's URL doesn't sit under any menu item, name the parent too with crumbParent:

<?php $this->extend('master') ?>

<?php $this->section('crumbParent') ?><?= lang('Tools.logsModTitle') ?><?php $this->endSection() ?>
<?php $this->section('crumb') ?><?= esc($logFilePretty) ?><?php $this->endSection() ?>

docs.title: Dashboard Cells
docs.text:
You can customize the dashboard with the use of view cells. You can specify which cells to display by editing the Bonfire\Dashboard\Config\Dashboard config class;

class Dashboard extends BaseConfig
{
    public array $cells = [
        'Bonfire\Widgets\Cells\WidgetCells::stats',
        'Bonfire\Widgets\Cells\WidgetCells::logs',
        'Bonfire\Widgets\Cells\WidgetCells::charts',
    ];
}

The cells make up the default layout of the Dashboard, in the order listed. You can comment out any class to have it not show. The stats, logs and charts cells that come on by default stand for the stats, log and chart widgets: those are not on the default layout, and admins add them from the palette. Every other cell becomes one full-width widget with the id cell: plus its Class::method, which admins can move, size or remove when they customize their dashboard. For more control over a widget's title, icon, sizes or permission, write a dashboard widget instead, as Quick Links now is.

docs.title: Creating the Cell
docs.text:
The cells are very simple class methods that return the HTML or view() results:

class ShopCells
{
    /**
     * Lists the orders waiting to ship.
     */
    public function openOrders()
    {
        return view('Shop\Views\open_orders', [
            'orders' => model(OrderModel::class)->open(),
        ]);
    }
}

Add 'Shop\Cells\ShopCells::openOrders' to $cells and it becomes the widget cell:Shop\Cells\ShopCells::openOrders.

docs.title: Dashboard Widgets
docs.text: Anything an admin can place on the dashboard is a widget. Stats, charts and the cells in Dashboard.cells become widgets on their own. For full control, implement Bonfire\Dashboard\DashboardWidget and register it from your module's initAdmin(). Bonfire's own Quick Links is built this way (Bonfire\Dashboard\Widgets\QuickLinksWidget).

docs.title: Writing a widget
docs.text:
use Bonfire\Dashboard\DashboardWidget;
use Bonfire\Dashboard\Size;
use Bonfire\Dashboard\SizeRange;
use Bonfire\Dashboard\WidgetField;
use Bonfire\Dashboard\WidgetValues;

class OpenOrders implements DashboardWidget
{
    public function id(): string { return 'shop:openOrders'; }
    public function title(): string { return 'Open orders'; }
    public function icon(): string { return 'fas fa-cart-shopping'; }
    public function group(): string { return 'Shop'; }
    public function description(): string { return 'Orders waiting to ship'; }
    public function sizes(): SizeRange { return new SizeRange(Size::Half, Size::Quarter, Size::TwoThirds); }
    public function permission(): ?string { return 'shop.orders'; }

    public function fields(): array
    {
        return [
            WidgetField::number('limit', 'Orders to show', default: 5, min: 1, max: 20),
            WidgetField::toggle('showTotals', 'Show totals', default: true),
        ];
    }

    public function render(WidgetValues $values): string
    {
        return view('Shop\Views\open_orders', [
            'orders'     => model(OrderModel::class)->open($values->get('limit')),
            'showTotals' => $values->get('showTotals'),
        ]);
    }
}
  • id is stored in admins' saved layouts, so keep it unique and never change it. Prefix it with your module's name.
  • group is the library heading it is listed under: your module's name. The library lists modules in name order. The older type keys quickLinks, stats, charts and custom still work, each under its own heading.
  • sizes is the width it starts at, then the smallest and largest an admin may pick, from Size::Quarter, Third, Half, TwoThirds and Full.
  • permission hides the widget from admins who lack it, in the library and on the dashboard, and drops it from layouts they save. null shows it to every admin.
  • fields are the settings admins may change for the widget on their own dashboard. Return [] when it has none, and its edit-mode tools offer no settings.
  • render is called only when the widget is on the viewer's dashboard, so it may run queries. It gets the value of each field as the viewer placed it.

docs.title: Settings
docs.text:
Each WidgetField is one setting, drawn in the widget's settings panel. Bonfire draws the form, checks what is posted, stores each admin's values with their layout, and hands render() the result. Read a value with $values->get('name'), not with setting().

Field Input Value WidgetField::toggle($name, $label, default: …) A switch bool WidgetField::number($name, $label, default: …, min: …, max: …, step: …) A number box int, or float when step is a fraction; kept within min and max WidgetField::choice($name, $label, $options, default: …) Segmented buttons, or a select for more than four options One of the keys of $options (value => label) WidgetField::text($name, $label, default: …) A text box string, trimmed, at most 255 characters

Every field also takes an optional description: shown under its label. A placed widget uses each field's default until an admin changes it. Only values that differ from the default are stored, so changing the default in code later reaches every admin who left the field alone. A value that is not of the field's type, a choice the field does not offer, or the name of a field the widget no longer declares is dropped when the layout is saved, and ignored when it is rendered.

docs.title: Registering it
docs.text:
public function initAdmin()
{
    service('dashboard')->register(new OpenOrders());
}

A registered widget is not part of the default layout: admins add it from the widget library, or a site admin puts it on the site default. To ship it on the default layout, add its id to the $layout of your Config\Dashboard.

docs.title: From the older APIs
docs.text:
The older ways of adding to the dashboard still work. Each becomes a widget with an id made from its kind and its own id:

You have It becomes Id Notes A StatsItem added to service('widgets')->widget('stats') A stat card, listed under 'module' => '…', else Stats stats: + its id Pass 'permission' => '…' to hide it from admins who lack it. A ChartsItem added to service('widgets')->widget('charts') A chart, listed under 'module' => '…', else Charts charts: + its id Its cssClass sets its default size. Takes 'permission' too. A view cell listed in Dashboard.cells A full-width widget, listed under Custom cell: + its Class::method No permission. Write a widget for more control.

A stats or chart item stores the query of addValue(), addValueByFreeQuery() or addDataset() and runs it when its value or data is first read: only when the dashboard renders it, for a viewer who holds its permission. A widget of your own gets the same for free by doing its work in render().

To move one of these to a widget of your own, give the new widget the id it had (for example stats:openOrders), so saved layouts keep it in place, and stop adding the old item. Quick Links did the same: it keeps the id cell:Bonfire\Dashboard\DashboardCells::quickLinks, so installs whose Dashboard.cells still lists that cell show it once, where it was.

docs.title: Filters
docs.text: Every collection of items needs to be filtered at some point. Unless you're building a photo gallery or an ecommerce site this might be when presenting posts, users, pages, etc in the admin area. Filtering allows you to specify which columns can be filtered and then pass your model to a view cell that takes care of handling the display of the filters for you. This ensures a consistent look and functionality in the UI while providing the least amount of work when you need to create a UI in a hurry.

docs.title: Specifying Filterable Columns
docs.text:
You specify the available filters within your Model, using a class property named filters.

protected $filters = [
    'column_name' => [
        'title' => 'Column Title',
        'type' => 'radio',
        'options' => ['one' => 'Option 1', 'two' => 'Option 2']
    ],
    'column_two' => [
        'title' => 'Column Title',
        'options' => 'methodName'
    ]
];

The key of each array element is the name of the column that you wish to filter on. The column must be within the table for the model (see below for other options). It is then described by an array with the keys title, options, and optional key type. Title is the display title for that group of options. The options value is typically an array of keys and their display values that the column should be filtered by. The keys must match valid values within the database. Key type signifies if the filter should be composed of checkboxes (default) or radio's. If it is omitted, the default value checkbox would be assumed. In case type => radio is specified, the last option in the options array will be pre-selected in the filter UI, so it should probably contain value representing all entries.

Sometimes you need to pull values from a config file, or another table, etc, in order to provide the list of options. In this case, you can use the string methodName where methodName is a method within the model to call that returns the list of options.

docs.title: Implementing the Filters
docs.text:
If all the columns match directly to columns within the model's database table, then you can make use of the Filterable trait, which implements a basic filter() method for you.

Since model's can get crowded with test data, filter data, custom methods, events, and more, you can split out the filter functionality into a new class that extends the model, placing your custom filter logic within that class.

use App\UserModel;
use Bonfire\Traits\Filterable;

class UserFilter extends UserModel
{
    use Filterable;

    public $filters = [
        ...
    ];

    /**
     * A computed options function
     */
    protected function computeFilterA()
    {
        //
    }
}

docs.title: Complex Filter Columns
docs.text:
There are many times that you'll need to show options that don't directly relate to the model at hand. In this case you must override the filter() method on the model. Within that method you must handle all of the cases for the options you provided manually, returning the query object.

public function filter(array $params)
{
    $query = $this->builder();

    if (isset($params['foo']) && ! empty($params['foo'])) {
        $query->whereIn('foo', $params['foo']);
    }

    return $query;
}

docs.title: Displaying Filters in the Admin
docs.text: There are 4 parts that are needed to get a working, filterable list of resources in the admin area.

docs.title: The Route
docs.text:
The main route for your resource list page must support both GET and POST methods.

$routes->match(['GET', 'POST'], 'users', 'UserController::list', ['as' => 'user-list']);

The controller should then choose between sending either a full HTML page for a regular GET request, or just sending back the table for ajax requests issued via HTMX. You might do it something like:

public function list()
{
    $userModel = model('UserFilter');

    // Performs the actual filtering of the results.
    $userModel->filter($this->request->getPost('filters'));

    $view = $this->request->hasHeader('HX-Request')
        ? $this->viewPrefix .'_table'
        : $this->viewPrefix .'list';

    return $this->render($view, [
        'headers' => [
            'email' => 'Email',
            'name' => 'Name',
            'groups' => 'Groups',
            'last_login' => 'Last Login'
        ],
        'showSelectAll' => true,
        'users' => $userModel->paginate(setting('Site.perPage')),
        'pager' => $userModel->pager,
    ]);
}

docs.title: The View
docs.text:
Within your view there are 3 things to do.

First, ensure that the table with your resource list is wrapped in a div that uses some Alpine.js to attach a filtered status of false to the div. This creates a variable that determines whether the filters list is shown or not.

Second, insert the x-filter-link component into the top of that div. This provides the link that will show/hide the list of filters. This component toggles the filtered value above between true and false.

Finally, call the renderList view cell which inserts the HTML for the list of options, all wrapped in a form that calls your controller method via AJAX and updates the list of items without a page refresh, using some htmx magic. When calling this, you must supply the ID of the div that surrounds the table of results as the target.

Here's how this is used for the list of users within Bonfire.

<div x-data="{filtered: false}">
    <x-filter-link />

    <div class="row">
        <!-- List Users -->
        <div class="col order-2 order-md-1" id="content-list">
            <?= $this->include('Bonfire\Users\Views\_table') ?>
        </div>

        <!-- Filters -->
        <div class="col-auto order-1 order-md-2" x-show="filtered" x-transition.duration.240ms>
            <?= view_cell('Bonfire\Libraries\Cells\Filters::renderList 'model=UserFilter target=#content-list') ?>
        </div>
    </div>
</div>

Note that the id of the eleent that contains the included table should be with id="content-list" as it this id is the default target for content replacements by the pager and the filter.

For the admin design's list footer ("Showing X of Y · Previous / Next", loaded through htmx), render the pager with the bonfire_list_hx template inside the replaced element: <?= $pager->links('default', 'bonfire_list_hx') ?>. It takes its hx-target from an ancestor, so put hx-target="#content-list" on an element that wraps the list.

docs.title: The Recycler
docs.text:
The Recycler provides an area where users can browse objects that have been deleted and either restore or purge them. The models for these resources must have soft deletes enabled. By default, only users are displayed here. 

// In the model:
protected $useSoftDeletes = true;

docs.title: Registering A Resource
docs.text:
The Recycler must be told which models it should display. You do not need to do anything special with a model before registering. A module registers its resources in the initAdmin() method of its Module.php: 

public function initAdmin()
{
    service('recycler')->register('photos', 'Photos', PhotoModel::class, [
        'title', 'caption',
    ]);
}

The arguments are, in order:

alias is what you would use to specify the default resource to show when visiting the Recycler, and is part of the URLs for restoring and purging.

label is the name as it should be displayed to the users.

model is the fully qualified classname of the model to get this resource's data from.

columns is an array of database column names for this resource that will be displayed on the Recycler table. This information should only be what is needed to allow someone to find the correct record.

An app can also add a resource, or replace how a module's resource is displayed, within app/Config/Recycler.php. An entry here wins over a module's registration with the same alias:

public $resources = [
    'users' => [
        'label' => 'Users',
        'model' => App\Models\UserModel::class,
        'columns' => [
            'username', 'first_name', 'last_name', 'email'
        ]
    ],
];

docs.title: Localization of Column names in Recycler
docs.text:
To localize the column names, an array recycler should be created in the module's language file, named after the $resource['label'] value (with the .php extension (in case of label 'Users' – Users.php). The array should have sub-keys label and columns, with each column name corresponding $resource['columns'] array value. Example for module Users:

    'recycler' => [
        'label'     => 'Users',
        'columns'   => [
            'id'           => 'ID',
            'username'     => 'User Name',
            'first_name'   => 'Name',
            'last_name'    => 'Surname',
            'email'        => 'Email',
        ],
    ],

If Recycler finds the localized strings, it will use them. Otherwise the original DB column names (capitalized, undescore replaced with space) will be used.

docs.title: Changing How A Model Is Recycled
docs.text:
The Recycler does three things with a resource: it lists the deleted records, restores one, and purges one. By default it lists the records through the model's soft delete field, ordered by the date they were deleted and returned as arrays; restores by setting that field to null; and purges by deleting the record through the model. It uses the primary key and soft delete field of the model, whatever they are called. It will only restore or purge a record that is in the Recycler.

To change any of the three, have the model implement the matching interface from Bonfire\Recycler\Interfaces. Implement only the ones you need. A method with the right name on a model that does not implement the interface is not called.

docs.title: Modifying the Recycler Query
docs.text:
While the basics mentioned above cannot be changed without breaking functionality, you can add requirements, or specify the fields to select, etc. Implement CustomRecyclerQuery and its setupRecycler() method. It doesn't take any arguments, and should return the modified model.

Here is an example from the UserModel that pulls in the email field from the auth_identities table. 

class UserModel extends ShieldUsers implements CustomRecyclerQuery
{
    public function setupRecycler(): static
    {
        return $this->select("users.*, 
            (SELECT secret 
                from auth_identities 
                where user_id = users.id
                    and type = 'email_password'
                order by last_used_at desc 
                limit 1
            ) as email
       ");
    }
}

docs.title: Overriding the Restore
docs.text:
You may override the default handling of the restore process if you have needs outside simply setting the deleted_at date to null. Implement CustomRecyclerRestore and its recyclerRestore() method. It only accepts a single argument, the record primary key, and returns whether the record was restored. 

public function recyclerRestore(int $id): bool
{
    return $this->where('id', $id)
        ->set('deleted_at', null)
        ->update();
}

docs.title: Overriding the Purge
docs.text:
You may override the default handling of the purge process if you have needs outside simply deleting the record. Implement CustomRecyclerPurge and its recyclerPurge() method. It only accepts a single argument, the record primary key, and returns whether the record was purged.

public function recyclerPurge(int $id): bool
{
    return (bool) $this->delete($id, true);
}

docs.title: Resource Tabs
docs.text:
Resource tabs are the tabs that are displayed when editing a resource, like an individual User or User Group. They make it possible for you to easily integrate other tabs onto a user without editing the core theme.

Adding a new tab is typically done from the Module.php for your module. You only need 3 pieces of information to create a new tab: a title, the URL to send them to, and (optionally) a permission to check against to see if they can see the tab or not.

use \Bonfire\Resources\ResourceTab;

public function initAdmin() 
{
    service('resourceTabs')->addTabFor('user', new ResourceTab([
        'title' => 'Permissions',
        'url' => 'users/(id)/permissions',
        'permission' => 'users.edit'
    ]));
}

The title is what is displayed to the user on the tab itself.

If it is set, permission will check the current user against that permission. If they have the permission then the tab will display, otherwise it will not be rendered.

When setting the URL there are a few things to note:

  1. The ADMIN_AREA constant will be prefixed to the URl you provide.
  2. To represent the ID of the resource you want to provide the tab to, use the (id) placeholder. This will be replaced by the ID of the current user being edited, by analyzing the current URL.

As an example, assuming you were on the current url /admin/users/123, the above URL would be /admin/users/123/permissions.

docs.title: Search
docs.text: Bonfire provides a flexible search system that is highlighted on all areas of the admin area. In order to make this as powerful as possible, any module may integrate into the search results, both by adding filters for the Advanced Search form, and by providing results that will be displayed.

docs.title: Providing Search Results
docs.text:
The most basic integration is to register your module as a search provider. This is done by creating a class at the root of your module's code called SearchProvider. It must extend Bonfire\Search\Interfaces\SearchProviderInterface and fill in a few small methods. Below is an example search provider for module Users.

<?php

namespace Bonfire\Users;

use Bonfire\Search\Interfaces\SearchProviderInterface;
use Bonfire\Users\Models\UserModel;

class SearchProvider extends UserModel implements SearchProviderInterface
{
    /**
     * Performs a primary search for just this resource.
     *
     * @param string     $term
     * @param int        $limit
     * @param array|null $post
     *
     * @return array
     */
    public function search(string $term, int $limit = 10, array $post = null): array
    {
        return $this->select('users.*')
            ->distinct()
            ->join('auth_identities', 'auth_identities.user_id = users.id', 'inner')
            ->like('first_name', $term, 'right', true, true)
            ->orlike('last_name', $term, 'right', true, true)
            ->orLike('username', $term, 'right', true, true)
            ->orLike('secret', $term, 'both', true, true)
            ->orderBy('first_name', 'asc')
            ->findAll($limit);
    }

    /**
     * Returns the name of the resource.
     *
     * @return string
     */
    public function resourceName(): string
    {
        return 'users';
    }

    /**
     * Returns a URL to the admin area URL main list
     * for this resource.
     *
     * @return string
     */
    public function resourceUrl(): string
    {
        return ADMIN_AREA .'/users';
    }

    /**
     * Returns the name of the view to use when
     * displaying the list of results for this
     * resource type.
     *
     * @return string
     */
    public function resultView(): string
    {
        return 'Search/users';
    }
}

search()

Given the search term it will return an array of any search results for this resource type. You'll see this SearcProvider extends the UserModel. It is not necessary to do so, but is a simple way to get access to the model features when you need them.

If you want the search to find not only the data from the main table, but also the related meta info (see User Meta Info), you should:

  1. Put a property $includeMetaFieldsInSearech into the module config file (example for app/Config/Users.php, since, suppose, we want to be able to search for users by their blog urls, which we keep in the meta_info table):

        public $includeMetaFieldsInSearech = [
    'blog',
    ];

  2. Employ Bonfire\Core\Traits\SearchInMeta trait: put use Bonfire\Core\Traits\SearchInMeta; before the SearchProvider class declaration and use SearchInMeta after the class declaration;

  3. Write the search() method employing the trait methods joinMetaInfo and orLikeInMetaInfo() when constructing the query:

    public function search(string $term, int $limit = 10, ?array $post = null): array
{
    $query = $this->select('users.*')->distinct();
    $query->join('auth_identities', 'auth_identities.user_id = users.id', 'inner');

    $searchInMeta = setting('Users.includeMetaFieldsInSearech');

    if (!empty($searchInMeta)) {
        // first argument is the resource entity name, second – the DB table name
        $query->joinMetaInfo('Bonfire\Users\User', 'users');
    }

    $query->like('first_name', $term, 'right', true, true)
        ->orlike('last_name', $term, 'right', true, true)
        ->orLike('username', $term, 'right', true, true)
        ->orLike('secret', $term, 'both', true, true);

    if (!empty($searchInMeta)) {
        foreach ($searchInMeta as $metaField) {
            // here syntax almost exactly like that of orLike()
            $query->orLikeInMetaInfo($metaField, $term, 'both', true, true);
        }
    }

    $query->orderBy('first_name', 'asc');

    return $query->findAll($limit);
}

resourceName()

The name of the resource. This is displayed as a header on the search results page where it shows the top 10 results from all search providers.

resourceUrl()

Returns the relative URL to the main page for this resource. In this case it takes you to the list of users.

resultView()

Returns the name of the view that should be used to display the results on the overview page. This MUST be in the Admin theme folder in order to be found. This can be a fairly straight-forward view file:

<table class="table table-hover">
    <?= $this->setData(['headers' => [
        'email' => 'Email',
        'username' => 'Username',
        'groups' => 'Groups',
        'last_active' => 'Last Active'
    ]])->include('_table_head') ?>
    <tbody>
    <?php service('actions')->for('users')->showing($rows) ?>
    <?php foreach($rows as $user) : ?>
        <tr>
            <?= view('Bonfire\Users\Views\_row_info', ['user' => $user]) ?>
        </tr>
    <?php endforeach ?>
    </tbody>
</table>

docs.title: View Components
docs.text:
View Components (or just Components) allow you to create custom HTML elements to use within your views. The main description of their use and creating new ones is described within the Building Sites section of the guide. This page lists the components that are available within the default Admin theme.

Escape attribute values with esc() (title="<?= esc($user->name()) ?>"), as you would any HTML attribute. The renderer decodes them and the component escapes them again on output, so a quote in the data can't end the attribute early. On a paired tag (<x-…>…</x-…>) a value can't contain >. Slots are HTML and are output as given.

docs.title: Page structure
docs.text:
<x-page-head>

The page header. Give it a title and it renders the design's head: an <h1>, an optional count badge or subtitle, an optional back link (backLabel names it, defaulting to "Back"), and the slot as actions on the right.

<x-page-head title="Users" count="<?= $total ?>">
    <a href="<?= url_to('user-new') ?>" class="btn btn-primary">New user</a>
</x-page-head>

<x-page-head title="<?= esc($user->displayName()) ?>" back="<?= esc(site_url(ADMIN_AREA . '/users')) ?>" backLabel="<?= esc(lang('Users.usersModTitle')) ?>" />

Without a title it wraps the slot as before, so existing <x-page-head><h2>…</h2></x-page-head> headers keep working.

<x-admin-box>

A card section. The optional title and description render a header. Setting rows and tables inside it run edge to edge; put buttons in a <div class="bf-card-footer"> as the last child for a footer.

<x-admin-box title="Site" description="How the site presents itself.">
    …
</x-admin-box>

<x-tabs>

Underline tabs. The slot holds Bootstrap nav-item list items, so service('resourceTabs')->renderTabsFor() output fits in it.

<x-tabs>
    <li class="nav-item"><a class="nav-link active" href="<?= $user->adminLink() ?>">Details</a></li>
    <?= service('resourceTabs')->renderTabsFor('user') ?>
</x-tabs>

<x-settings-layout>

The frame of a settings page: a "Settings" page head, a sub-nav of the sidebar's settings collection (only the pages the user may open, the current one marked), and the slot beside it. Register your module's settings page in that collection and wrap the page in it.

<x-settings-layout>
    <form action="<?= site_url(ADMIN_AREA . '/settings/blog') ?>" method="post">
        <?= csrf_field() ?>
        <x-admin-box title="Posts">…</x-admin-box>
        <x-save-bar />
    </form>
</x-settings-layout>

<x-sidebar>

This is the main view that renders the sidebar and all links within it.

docs.title: Settings forms
docs.text:
<x-setting-row>

A label and description on the left, the control (the slot) on the right. Wraps on narrow screens. for points the label at the control's id.

<x-setting-row label="Site name" description="Shown in the admin." for="siteName">
    <input type="text" class="form-control" id="siteName" name="siteName" value="<?= esc($siteName) ?>">
</x-setting-row>

<x-switch>

An accessible role="switch" checkbox. A hidden input posts offValue (default 0) when it is off; value (default 1) posts when it is on. Give it an empty offValue to post nothing when off, as for an array name like permissions[] that should hold only the checked values. checked turns it on unless it is empty, 0 or false; label becomes its aria-label. Any other attribute (id, x-model, disabled, …) goes on the checkbox.

<x-switch name="siteOnline" label="Site online" checked="<?= setting('Site.siteOnline') ? '1' : '' ?>" />
<x-switch name="permissions[]" offValue value="users.edit" checked="<?= $canEdit ? '1' : '' ?>" />

<x-segmented>

A radio group styled as a segmented control. options is a JSON object of value => label; wrap it in single quotes.

<x-segmented name="timeFormat" label="Time format" value="<?= $timeFormat ?>"
    options='<?= json_encode(['g:i A' => '12-hour', 'H:i' => '24-hour'], JSON_HEX_APOS) ?>' />

<x-save-bar>

A sticky "Unsaved changes · Discard · Save" bar for long forms. Put it inside the <form>: it appears once a field changes, Discard resets the form, and Save submits it. save relabels the Save button. Without JavaScript it is always shown, so the form can still be submitted.

<form method="post" action="…">
    …
    <x-save-bar save="Save settings" />
</form>

docs.title: Lists
docs.text:
<x-chip>

A pill filter with an optional count. With an href it is a link (active marks the current one). With a name it is a radio input for a filter form, checked when active; give the chips one name and each its own value. With neither it is a toggle button. Other attributes (hx-get, hx-target, …) pass through.

<x-chip label="Admins" count="3" href="?group=admin" active="<?= $group === 'admin' ? '1' : '' ?>" />

<x-chip name="role" value="admin" label="Admins" count="3" active="<?= $role === 'admin' ? '1' : '' ?>" />

<x-status>

A coloured dot and a label. tone is ok, warn, danger, info or muted (the default).

<x-status tone="ok" label="Active" />

<x-empty-state>

A centered title and optional hint for a list with nothing in it.

<x-empty-state title="No users match" hint="Try a different search or group." />

<x-selection-bar>

A sticky bar showing "N selected" while any row checkbox (tbody input[type=checkbox]) in its form is checked. The slot holds the bulk actions; the ✕ clears the selection.

<form method="post">
    <?= csrf_field() ?>
    <table class="table">…</table>
    <x-selection-bar>
        <x-bulk-actions list="users" />
    </x-selection-bar>
</form>

<x-bulk-actions>

The bulk actions of the list, as buttons that post the form's checked selects[]. Place it inside <x-selection-bar>.

<x-row-actions>

A row's menu: its slot (links like Edit), then the row actions of the list for the record id.

<x-row-actions list="users" id="<?= $user->id ?>">
    <li><a href="<?= $user->adminLink() ?>" class="dropdown-item">Edit</a></li>
</x-row-actions>

<x-confirm-dialog> and <x-action-run>

Both sit once in the Admin layout (master.php). <x-confirm-dialog> asks before actions, hx-confirm requests and data-confirm links and buttons go ahead (see Confirmation), and renders the form <x-row-actions> submits, so row actions need it even without JavaScript. <x-action-run>, inside the toasts, shows the progress of an action run just queued.

docs.title: Buttons and filters
docs.text:
<x-button>

This is used within the admin forms to add pre-styled buttons (configurable via attributes color (any pre-defined Bootstrap 5 color, like primary, secondary, success, etc., defaulting to primary) and type (defaults to submit, but can also be reset, button, etc.). id, name and onclick are passed on as well.

<x-button-container>

Wrapper for form button area enforcing uniform margins.

<x-module-title>

A muted line of text for page headers.

<x-filter-link>

This is used by the Filters system to show the link that display or hides the filters in a resource list page.

<x-filter-list>

This is the box that wraps the list of filters in a resource list page.

docs.title: Widgets
docs.text: Widgets are elements that display information on the dashboard. They are either a small informational card, or a chart of some sort.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text: Some settings are available in the administration settings area. Each type of widget has its own specific settings, which can be used to specify which information is displayed for the widget, as well as whether it's animated, where labels are displayed, etc.

docs.title: Your own dashboard widget
docs.text: Implement Bonfire\Dashboard\DashboardWidget and register it with service('dashboard')->register(). See Dashboard Widgets, which also maps the stats, charts and cells below onto widgets.

docs.title: Statistic widget
docs.text:
The first widget is the statistics widget, which is just a counter with a shortcut that allows me to open the list of elements of a module. It could be used to display a year-to-day revenue at a glance, total number of users in the system, new users this month, or any other simple statistic.

Adding a new widget is done by editing the initAdmin method of your Module.php file, similar to adding a menu:

// Settings widgets stats on dashboard
$widgets = service('widgets');
$users = new UserModel();
$statsItem = new StatsItem([
    'bgColor' => 'bg-blue',
    'title'   => 'Users',
    'value'   => $users->countAll(),
    'id'      => 'countAllUsers643',
    'url'     => ADMIN_AREA . '/users',
    'faIcon'  => 'fa fa-user',
]);
$widgets->widget("stats")->collection('stats')->addItem($statsItem);

bgColor

bgColor represents the background color of the widget. The available options are:

- bg-blue
- bg-red
- bg-orange
- bg-light
- bg-dark
- bg-inverse
- bg-indigo
- bg-purple
- bg-pink
- bg-yellow
- bg-green
- bg-teal
- bg-lime
- bg-cyan
- bg-white
- bg-gray
- bg-gray-dark

title

The title of the widget displayed at the top left

value

The value of the widget displayed under the title: typically the total number of records.

However, more elaborate data can be passed as a string, like an html table with tabulated data. See how that is done in src/Users/Module.php with a private method buildTableUsersByGroup(). value can also be passed to the stats item by a standard addValue() method, see the same file for an example.

id

A uniwue widget ID throughout application (make it descriptive and add extra symbols to make sure the uniqueness).

url

The address that displays the list of objects on your module. It will be associated with the word "view detail"

faIcon

The FontAwesome icon

docs.title: Fetching data only when it is shown
docs.text: addValue() and addValueByFreeQuery() store their query and run it when the value is first read. The dashboard reads it only for a widget in the viewer's layout whose permission they hold, so a stats item costs nothing on other pages. A value you pass directly runs whenever your module boots: build that in a widget's render() instead (see Dashboard Widgets).

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
All settings are available in the admin settings area.

In the administration settings area, you can also choose to: - Display the "View Detail" link

docs.title: Charts widget
docs.text:
Adding a new chart widget is done in the initAdmin method of your Module.php file, similar to adding a menu:

$statsItem = new ChartsItem([
    'title'    => 'User classification by group',
    'type'     => 'line',
    'id'       => 'usersByGroupLine123',
    'cssClass' => 'col-6',
]);
$statsItem->addDataset('auth_groups_users', 'group', 'user_id');
$widgets->widget('charts')->collection('charts')->addItem($statsItem);

title

The title of the chart displayed at the top center

type

The type of chart. The available options are: 

- line
- bar
- doughnut
- pie
- polarArea

id

A uniwue widget ID throughout application (make it descriptive and add extra symbols to make sure the uniqueness).

cssClass

Set the width of the chart. Examples options are: 

- col-3
- col-6
- col-9
- col-12

addDataset(string $tableName, string $groupField, string $countField, string $selectMode = 'count')

Currently, only one dataset can be added to the chart. The required parameters are:

  • Name of the table
  • Grouping field
  • Field to count

It is possible to indicate a fourth parameter to choose the counting mode; the possible values are:

- count
- avg
- max
- min
- sum
  • if indicate count then selectCount($field) is executed
  • if indicate avg then selectAvg($field) is executed
  • if indicate max then selectMax($field) is executed
  • if indicate min then selectMin($field) is executed
  • if indicate sum then selectSum($field) is executed

docs.title: Log activity widget
docs.text:
The Log activity widget charts the last days up to today, one stacked bar per day's log file, split into Error, Warning, Info and Debug entries. CRITICAL, ALERT and EMERGENCY entries count as Error, and NOTICE entries count as Info. Each bar links to that log file, days without a log file show a thin line, and the headline counts the errors across the days shown.

It is built in (Bonfire\Tools\Widgets\LogActivity, id logs:logActivity). Only users with the logs.view permission can add it to their dashboard, and the log files are only read when it is on the dashboard being shown.

docs.title: Building Sites
docs.text:
While Bonfire focuses on providing a powerful backend area for your sites, a number of the provided tools can be used within your front-end sites with minimal work. This includes some helper functions for working with dates, a user consent framework for helping you comply with some of the global privacy laws, like GDPR, new tools to build your views with, and more.

Much like any CodeIgniter application, your code will typically live in the /app folder, utilizing the standard Controllers, Models, Views, and other folders for your code. You can, of course, located modules anywhere you wish as long as the autoloader can find it. None of this changes using Bonfire. All of Bonfire's code is kept in the vendor folder, where it will not conflict with your application's code. There are new config files to keep an eye out for.

There is also an example frontpage with a full-blown App theme bonfire2-frontpage-theme for you to look at.

docs.text:
Bonfire provides a few helper functions that are always available for your use, such as app_date for formatting dates.

Read more about Common Functions

docs.title: Alerts
docs.text:
Bonfire uses Tatter\Alerts to provide support for simple alerts. The usage is simple: 

alert('success', 'Your message goes here.');

This displays a green message that appears in the top-right corner of the admin area. The first argument (success) specifies a Bootstrap alert type that is added to the class automatically to specify how it looks. The second argument is the content that should be in the alert and can be a single string or an array of strings to apply multiple alerts.

Additionally, you can use flash messages in the session to trigger alerts. This would typically be used during a redirect: 

return redirect()->back()->with('message', 'It worked!');
return redirect()->back()->with('error', 'Did not work');
return redirect()->back()->with('error', ['not good', 'nope', 'cannot do it']);

When an array is used it will display a new alert for each element in the array.

You can adjust which session variables are checked and their class mapping using the Alerts config file. Read more in the docs at the repo linked above.

docs.title: Including Assets
docs.text: As elaborated in Assets Management, Bonfire provides a simple assets system that was created to serve CSS/JS assets from anywhere and to easily handle browser caching/cache-busting with updated assets.

docs.title: Linking to assets
docs.text:
Within your views you can link to assets anywhere within your project with the asset() or asset_link() helper function. asset_link() takes two arguments. The first is the path to the file to load. The first segment of this path must be one of the defined $folders in the configuration file Assets.php. The rest of the path would be based on the actual file structure within that location. For the App theme, a folder has been defined called app.

The second argument is the type of asset being loaded. Currently, it only supports css and js files.

<?= asset_link('app/css/admin.css', 'css') ?>
<?= asset_link('app/js/admin.js', 'js') ?>

The asset() function is similar, except it only returns the URL only.

<link rel="stylesheet" href="<?= asset('admin/css/admin.css', 'css') ?>" />
<script src="<?= asset('admin/js/admin.js', 'js') ?>"></script>

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text: Configuration of assets is detailed in the Assets Management page of Modules section.

docs.title: Common functions
docs.text:
Bonfire provides a helper function that is always available for your use.

app_date($date)

This helper will display a date based on the current settings in the General Settings page for date format and the application's current timezone. You can pass a string with the date, a DateTime object, or a CodeIgniter\i18n\Time instance as the first argument.

echo app_date('2021-01-15 15:35:00');
// outputs: 01/15/2021

$date = new DateTime('2021-01-15 15:35:00');
echo app_date($date);

$date = new CodeIgniter\i18n\Time('2021-01-15 15:35:00');
echo app_date($date);

You can include the time, formatted as specified in General Settings, by passing true as the second argument.

echo app_date($date, true);
// outputs: 01/15/2021 3:35 PM

You can further include the timezone by passing true as the third argument.

echo app_date($date, true, true);
// outputs: 01/15/2021 3:35 PM CST

docs.title: View Components
docs.text: View Components (or just Components) allow you to create custom HTML elements to use within your views.

docs.title: Self-Closing Tag Components
docs.text:
At their most basic, components serve as dynamic templates that allow you to reduce the typing in your application. This can help boil longer, complex sections down to a single HTML tag. This is especially useful with CSS utility frameworks like TailWind, or when using the utilities in Bootstrap 5, etc. Using components in these situations allows you to keep the style info in one place where making changes to one file changes every instance of the view throughout the application.

To create a component, simply create a new view file within the theme's Component directory, or the application's, app/Components directory.

A simple avatar image might look something like this: 

// app/Components/avatar.php
<img
  src="<?= $src ?? '' ?>"
  class="rounded-circle shadow-4"
  style="width: <?= $width ?? '150px' ?>;"
  alt="<?= $alt ?? '' ?>"
/>

When using the component within a view, you would insert a tag with x- prepended to the filename: 

<x-avatar src="<?= $user->avatarUrl() ?>" alt="<?= $user->name ?>" />

Any attributes provided when you insert the component like this are made available as variables within the component view. In this case, the $src and $alt attributes are passed to the component view, resulting in the following output: 

<img
  src="http://example.com/avatars/foo.jpg"
  class="rounded-circle shadow-4"
  style="width: 150px"
  alt="John Smith"
/>

docs.title: Components With Opening and Closing Tags
docs.text:
You can include the content within the opening and closing tags by inserting the reserved $slot variable: 

<x-green-button>Click Me!</x-green-button>
// app/Components/green-button.php
<button class="btn btn-success">
    <?= $slot ?>
</button>

docs.title: Controlled Components
docs.text:
Finally, you can create a class to add additional logic to the output for both self-closing tags and tags with content. The file must be in the same directory as the component view, and should have a name that is the PascalCase version of the filename, with 'Component' added to the end of it. Any attributes that you set on the custom element and any content within element will be passed to the class of the controlled component to be, optionally, processed by the component class and/or rendered by the comonent view file. The data you pass will be available within the class as it's $data property (the tag content – as $data['slot'] property).

A famous-qoutes component would have a view called famous-quotes.php and a controlling class called FamousQuotesComponent.php. The class must extend Bonfire\View\Component. The only requirement is that you implement a method called render().

Below are example files of a usable famous-quotes component, that can be included in any of these three ways:

<x-famous-quotes />
<x-famous-quotes seconds="30" />
<x-famous-quotes seconds="30">Famous Quotes</x-famous-quotes>

It's controlling class file FamousQuotesComponent.php:

namespace App\Components;

/**
 * This example controlled component allows to retrieve a random famous quote
 * from the ZenQuotes API and cache it for a specified number of seconds.
 * Number of seconds can be passed as a parameter to the component.
 * If you want to add a title to the component, you can pass it as a $slot variable.
 */
class FamousQuotesComponent extends \Bonfire\View\Component
{
    protected $defaultNoOfSeconds         = 600;
    protected string $famousQuotesAPINode = 'https://zenquotes.io/api/random';

    public function render(): string
    {
        return $this->renderView($this->view, $this->getFamousQuote());
    }

    public function getFamousQuote(): array
    {
        helper('cache');

        if (isset($this->data['seconds']) && is_numeric($this->data['seconds'])) {
            $this->data['seconds'] = (int) round($this->data['seconds'], 0);
        } else {
            $this->data['seconds'] = $this->defaultNoOfSeconds;
        }

        $cacheKey = 'famous_quote';

        if ($cachedQuote = cache($cacheKey)) {
            return $cachedQuote;
        }

        $response  = file_get_contents($this->famousQuotesAPINode);
        $quoteData = json_decode($response, true);

        if (isset($quoteData[0])) {
            $this->data['quote'] = [
                'text'   => $quoteData[0]['q'],
                'author' => $quoteData[0]['a'],
            ];

            cache()->save($cacheKey, $this->data, $this->data['seconds']);
        } else {
            $this->data['quote'] = [
                'text'   => 'Sucking at something is the first step to becoming sorta good at something.',
                'author' => 'Jake (from "Adventure Time")',
            ];
        }

        return $this->data;
    }
}

And it's view file famous-quotes.php:

<div class="card mb-3">
    <div class="card-header">
        <?= esc($slot ?? '') ?>
    </div>
    <div class="card-body mt-3">
        <p class="card-text text-center"><?= esc($quote['text']) ?></p>
        <footer class="blockquote-footer text-center"><em><?= esc($quote['author']) ?></em></footer>
    </div>
    <div class="card-footer" style="font-size:10px;">Cached for <?= esc($seconds) ?> seconds</div>
</div>

docs.title: Consent
docs.text: With the Global Data Protection Regulation and other data privacy regulations being put in place across the globe, you have various requirements as web developers that you didn't use to. The Consent module helps you manage collecting consent from the user before storing any cookies through an opt-in system for all non-required cookies. It provides the mechanism for displaying the consent form, and recording the user's preferences. A helper method, has_consent, is provided so that you can easily meet the consent requirements when building your site.

docs.title: Using the Helper
docs.text:
The helper is loaded automatically by the BaseController. As long as you extend the BaseController (or one of its children, like the AuthController) then you do not need to explicitly load the helper.

The helper can be used both within the views and the controllers to limit which services are called (like ad-tracking or analytics) and which cookies you set.

Within a view you might wrap Google Analytics tag withn a check against the performing consent: 

<?php if (has_consent('performing')) : ?>
<script>
    <!-- Global Site Tag (gtag.js) - Google Analytics -->
    ... (several lines of code) ...
</script>
<?php endif ?>

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
All settings are available in the Config\Consent class, or in the admin settings area.

$requireConsent

This determines whether the consent system is enabled or not. If true, the consent form will be automatically inserted into all front-end views by the Consent controller filter. If false, the consent system will not display and the helper will always return true. The default value is false;

$consentLength

The number of days before a visitor is asked for their consent again. The default value is 180 days (6 months).

$consentForm

The view that is displayed to site visitors that a) asks for their basic consent and b) allows them to accept/reject the various consents. The required consent is unable to be rejected and contains things like the Auth cookie that determines if you're logged in or not.

$consentFormStyles $consentFormScripts

The views that will be loaded that contain the CSS and Javascript, respectively. The contents of these views will be inserted into each page upon page load.

$policyUrl

A URL (either full or relative) that points to the page that details the cookie policy. On many sites this will be included in the Privacy Policy or Terms of Service pages, or similar.

$consents

This is an array of the initial consents that will be asked for in the Consent Form. Each array item includes the alias the consent can be checked with, and the following items:

  • name: The name as it is displayed to the visitors.
  • desc: The description of the consent that describes the purpose of the cookies/services and what might be no longer functional if the consent is rejected.

docs.title: Meta Info
docs.text:
Bonfire provides Entity-Attribute-Value style storage for additional data of entities without modifying the underlying models and database tables. By default, it can be used to add meta information to users, and it can also be used to store nad retrieve meta information for the entities managed by your own admin modules.

Once you configure meta info for a resource as described in the Meta Info page of Modules section, you can access and write extra data to an entity without the modifying the underlying resource database table:

// access your user entity
$user = model('UserModel')->find(5);

$url = $this->request->getPost('website_url');
// save meta field:
$user->saveMeta('website_url', $url);

// get all meta data
$meta = $user->allMeta();

// delete meta info entry
$user->deleteMeta('website_url');

// delete all meta info for an entry
$user->deletResouceMeta();

// update meta for a resource
$post = [
    'website_url' => 'https://example.com',
    'facebook_name' => 'johnny.rose'
];
$user->syncMeta($post);

See more examples and detailed documentation on Meta Info page.

docs.title: View Metadata
docs.text:
Bonfire provides a Metadata service that simplifies working with the meta information, scripts, and styles in your application.

$viewMeta = service('viewMeta');

// Add the page title
$viewMeta->setTitle('My Site');

// Add misc page meta data
$viewMeta->addMeta(['description' => 'This is the description of the page']);
$viewMeta->addMeta(['property' => 'og:title', 'content' => 'This is the title of the page']);

// Add link tags
$viewMeta->addLink(['rel' => 'canonical', 'href' => 'https://example.com/']);
$viewMeta->addLink(['rel' => 'icon', 'href' => 'favicon.ico', 'type' => 'image/x-icon']);

// Add script tags
$viewMeta->addScript(['src' => 'https://example.com/js/jquery.min.js']);
$viewMeta->addScript(['src' => 'https://example.com/js/bootstrap.min.js', 'type' => 'text/javascript']);

// Adding script blocks
$script = <<<TEXT
    // all your javscript code here
TEXT;
$viewMeta->addRawScript($script);

The addMeta, addLink and addScript methods all take an array of key value pairs. Each of the pairs will have all of the key/value pairs rendered as key=value within the tags, so you can fully customize what each one contains.

docs.title: Outputting the Metadata
docs.text:
Within your layouts you can use the render() method to render any of the data types.

// Render the title tag - <title>...</title>
<?= $viewMeta->render('title') ?>
// Get just the title value
<?= $viewMeta->title() ?>

// Render all meta tags
<?= $viewMeta->render('meta') ?>

// Render all link tags
<?= $viewMeta->render('link') ?>

// Render all script tags
<?= $viewMeta->render('script') ?>
<?= $viewMeta->render('rawScripts') ?>

docs.title: Settings
docs.text:
Bonfire provides a simple interface that you can use in place of calling config() to allow you to read and store config values in the database. If the value has not been updated and saved in the database then the original value from the config file will be used.

This allows you to save your application's default state as values in config files, all stored in version control, and still allows your users to override those settings once the site is live.

docs.title: Setup
docs.text: A migration is provided that will create the required settings table. It was run during by the Bonfire installation script. No other setup is needed.

docs.title: Usage
docs.text:
To retrieve a config value use the settings() helper method that is always loaded. 

// The same as config('App')->siteName;
$siteName = setting('App', 'siteName');
// or
$siteName = setting()->get('App', 'siteName');

In this case we used the short class name, App, which the config() method automatically locates within the app/Config directory. If it was from a module, it would be found there. Either way, the fully qualified name is automatically detected by the Settings class to keep values separated from config files that may share the same name but different namespaces.

To save a value, call the set() method on the settings class, providing the class name, the key, and the value. Note that boolean true/false will be converted to strings :true and :false when stored in the database, but will be converted back into a boolean when retrieved. Arrays and objects are serialized when saved, and unserialized when retrieved. 

setting()->set('App', 'siteName', 'My Great Site');

docs.title: Admin accent color
docs.text:
The admin theme's highlight color is the Site.adminAccent setting, a #rrggbb hex string that defaults to #D9622B. Admins change it under Settings → General. To set it from code:

setting('Site.adminAccent', '#2F6FEB');

Use the admin_accent() helper to read it. The helper always returns a valid hex color and falls back to the default when the stored value isn't one.

docs.title: Bonfire Application Structure
docs.text: Bonfire is an add-on to CodeIgniter 4, packaged as a set of modules and libraries that can be used together or independently. That means that all of its code lives within the vendor folder, leaving your app folder clean and uncluttered with boilerplate code. But there are a few files and folders that you should be aware of.

docs.title: Config files
docs.text:
Once installed, Bonfire will have copied several configuration files into your app/Config folder. These files are used to configure the various modules and libraries that Bonfire provides. You can modify these files to change the behavior of Bonfire. The following files are copied over:

  • Assets - Used to define how the Assets library should behave.
  • Auth, AuthGroups, AuthTokens - These files are part of the Shield authentication library and are used to define your initial user groups, permissions, and how the authentication system should behave.
  • Bonfire - This allows you to customize some views used by Bonfire, as well as define any additional modules it should know about and load, and allows you to modify the order of the default admin menu items.
  • Site - Allows you to define whether the site is online or in maintenance mode, set the site name, and more.
  • Themes - Determines which themes are available to the system, and some view component settings.
  • Consent - Defines how the Cookie Consent library should behave.
  • Dashboard - Allows you to define the widgets that should be displayed on the dashboard.
  • Recycler - Defines how the Recycler library should behave, and lets an app add or override its resources.
  • Users - Contains avatar settings, custom user fields, and more.

docs.title: /themes
docs.text:
A new folder is created in the project root that holds the view files that define a theme for Bonfire. Themes provide the basic structure of the web pages, including all of the information that surrounds the actual content. By default, it ships with three themes, admin, app, and auth.

  • The admin theme is what is used for the Bonfire admin area.
  • The app theme is extremely simple and is meant mostly as a semi-functional skeleton that you can leverage as a starting point for your app.
  • The auth theme is more a set of partials that are used for all of the authentication-related screens. You can specify which theme/layout it should extend.

docs.title: Change Log
docs.text:
This holds the change history for Bonfire as we lead up to a 1.0 release. It's not exhaustive, but should give you a good idea of the changes that have been made and how it might impact you.

IMPORTANT! Breaking changes are marked with words breaking change in parentheses right after the date.

docs.title: 29 October 2026
docs.text:
A Recently active dashboard widget (users:recentlyActive) lists the users active within the last 5 minutes, hour or 24 hours, most recent first, each linking to their account. It needs the users.list permission; add it from Add widget on the dashboard.

A Recent failed logins dashboard widget (users:failedLogins) lists the newest unsuccessful login attempts across all accounts, with the identifier, IP address and date. Attempts by a known user's email link to their Security tab for admins who may open it. It needs the users.view permission; add it from Add widget on the dashboard.

docs.title: 29 October 2026 (breaking change)
docs.text:
An action run's lifecycle now lives in service('actionRuns') (Bonfire\Actions\ActionRuns): dispatch() runs an action in the request or queues it, process() runs a queued run, and progress() and toast() look one up for the admin who started it. ActionRunModel now reads and writes status as a Bonfire\Actions\RunStatus enum in place of the strings queued, running, done and failed, so code that writes a status string to it must pass the enum. The Admin theme's <x-action-run> now calls service('actionRuns')->toast() rather than ActionRunModel; installs that published the Admin theme should copy the new themes/Admin/Components/action-run.php.

Picking an accent color swatch under Settings → General → Appearance now shows the save bar, so the new color can be saved. Before, only the color picker itself did.

docs.title: 28 October 2026
docs.text:
spark notify:breaking-changes used to keep its marker in a last-update.txt file inside the package folder, which composer update deleted together with the previous version, so it warned on every update. It now remembers the breaking change it last reported in writable/bonfire-breaking-changes.json: expect one more warning after this update, and none for changes you have already been shown.

The check also notices a note added to an existing (breaking change) heading, not only a new heading, and a fresh install no longer warns about changes that came before it. If writable/ is recreated on every deploy, move the marker with Config\Bonfire::$breakingChangeStateFile. See Updating Bonfire.

The dashboard's widget library now lists widgets by the module that adds them, in name order, in place of by type. A widget's group() gives its module's name; the type keys quickLinks, stats, charts and custom still work, each under its own heading. A StatsItem or ChartsItem takes 'module' => '…' (see Dashboard Widgets). With the library open, the page now widens by its width instead of narrowing the dashboard, where the screen has room.

The sidebar now shows Settings as a single link to the first settings page you may open, since the settings pages list one another in their own nav. A menu collection opts into this with setPageNav(). Installs that published the Admin theme keep the old expanding Settings menu until they copy the new themes/Admin/Components/sidebar.php.

Each admin can now change a dashboard widget's settings for their own dashboard: in edit mode, its sliders button opens them in a panel, and they are saved with the layout (see Customizing the Dashboard). Stat cards, charts and Log activity have settings; until an admin changes one, it follows the site-wide value in Settings → Widgets. Widgets declare their settings with fields(), a list of Bonfire\Dashboard\WidgetField, and get their values in render(WidgetValues $values); DashboardWidget::settingsUrl() is gone (see Dashboard Widgets).

The Log activity widget now shows a column for each of the last days up to today, with a thin line for days without a log file. Its Days to show setting (formerly Log files to show) keeps its saved value, and now defaults to 7.

Dashboard widgets can need a permission: pass 'permission' to a StatsItem or ChartsItem, and admins who lack it don't see it in the widget library or on their dashboard, nor is its data fetched for them. The built-in Users widgets need users.list and the Groups widgets groups.settings. Admins with widgets.settings can Save as site default from the dashboard's edit bar, and Reset site default in Settings → Widgets (see Customizing the Dashboard). The Settings → Widgets switches are now labelled as choosing which widgets are available. Quick Links is now a native widget, Bonfire\Dashboard\Widgets\QuickLinksWidget, registered by the Dashboard module under its old id, and no longer in the default Dashboard.cells; installs that still list Bonfire\Dashboard\DashboardCells::quickLinks show it once, in place. DashboardCells::quickLinks() is deprecated. Building widgets is documented in Dashboard Widgets.

docs.title: 28 October 2026 (breaking change)
docs.text:
